blocks.text: A 28-year-old at 14 weeks of gestation sits in the antenatal clinic. Her first baby was born at 29 weeks after spontaneous labour, and she had a cone biopsy of the cervix three years ago. She wants to know whether this will happen again and what can be done. The answer is a plan built on risk assessment, cervical surveillance and a handful of treatments that change the outcome for babies born early.

blocks.markdown:
**Definitions.** **Preterm birth** is birth before 37 completed weeks. By gestation it is subdivided into **extremely preterm** (under 28 weeks), **very preterm** (28 to under 32 weeks) and **moderate to late preterm** (32 to under 37 weeks). Preterm birth is the leading cause of neonatal death and of long-term neurodevelopmental disability. Roughly two-thirds follow spontaneous preterm labour or preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM), and the rest are iatrogenic, for example delivery for pre-eclampsia or fetal compromise.

**Risk factors.** The strongest is a **previous spontaneous preterm birth or late miscarriage**. Others: **short cervical length** (including after cone biopsy or large loop excision), multiple pregnancy, uterine anomaly, genital tract infection and intra-amniotic infection, polyhydramnios, antepartum haemorrhage, smoking and substance use, low body mass index, short interpregnancy interval, and extremes of maternal age. Many women who deliver preterm have no identifiable risk factor.

blocks.title: Tocolysis, antenatal corticosteroids and neuroprotection
blocks.text: Tocolysis is the use of drugs to suppress uterine contractions; it delays delivery by a short time (about 48 hours) and has not been shown to improve neonatal outcome by itself. Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage, necrotising enterocolitis and death. Magnesium sulfate given to the mother before very early delivery reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in the child.

blocks.markdown:
**Prevention.** Strategies depend on risk:

- **Pre-conception and antenatal**: smoking cessation, treating asymptomatic bacteriuria and symptomatic infections, optimising medical conditions and spacing pregnancies.
- **Surveillance** in high-risk women: transvaginal **cervical length** scans at defined gestations (for example from 16 to 24 weeks), and in symptomatic women fetal fibronectin or other tests to estimate risk of delivery within 7 days.
- **Interventions** for a short cervix in women with prior preterm birth or cervical surgery: **vaginal progesterone** and/or **cervical cerclage** (suture placed around the cervix), chosen by specialist assessment (follow current NICE and RCOG guidance).

**Management of threatened preterm labour** has four aims: (1) give **antenatal corticosteroids** (for example betamethasone 12 mg intramuscularly, two doses 24 hours apart, usually from about 24 weeks to 34 weeks; teaching example, check against current NICE/RCOG/local guidance), ideally with at least 24 hours before birth; (2) give **magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection** to women delivering before about 30 weeks (and consider up to 34 weeks); (3) consider **tocolysis** with nifedipine (or atosiban, an oxytocin receptor antagonist) in women with intact membranes to gain time for steroids and **in-utero transfer** to a unit with neonatal intensive care; (4) intrapartum prophylactic antibiotics against group B streptococcus. Tocolysis is not given if there is abruption, chorioamnionitis, fetal compromise or an intrauterine death. In PPROM, tocolysis is not recommended; antibiotics (for example erythromycin) are given to prolong pregnancy and reduce infection.

blocks.title: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 32 weeks
blocks.prompt: A 33-year-old at 32+0 weeks has a gush of clear fluid. Sterile speculum shows pooling of liquor. Contractions are absent, fetal heart rate and maternal observations are normal, and temperature is 36.9 C. Outline her management.

steps.text: Confirm the diagnosis clinically (pooling) and assess for contractions, infection (temperature, pulse, uterine tenderness, raised CRP or white cell count) and fetal wellbeing. Avoid digital examination.

Give antenatal corticosteroids (she is at 32 weeks, within the recommended range) and start oral erythromycin to delay delivery and reduce infection. Tocolysis is not recommended in PPROM, and there are no contractions anyway.

Monitor for chorioamnionitis and fetal compromise; plan delivery usually around 34 weeks if expectant management goes well, or earlier if infection or other indication arises. Arrange a unit with appropriate neonatal care.

blocks.answer: Steroids, erythromycin, no tocolysis, surveillance for infection, and planned delivery from about 34 weeks (or earlier if infection or fetal compromise); follow current NICE guidance.

blocks.markdown:
**Multiple pregnancy.** Twins arise from two eggs (**dizygotic**, always dichorionic diamniotic, DCDA) or from division of one fertilised egg (**monozygotic**). The timing of division determines chorionicity and amnionicity: roughly days 0 to 3 gives DCDA; days 4 to 8, monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA); days 8 to 12, monochorionic monoamniotic (MCMA); later division gives conjoined twins. **Chorionicity** is determined by ultrasound in the first trimester (11 to 14 weeks): a **lambda (twin peak) sign** at the placental junction indicates dichorionic, and a **T sign** indicates monochorionic diamniotic. It is the main determinant of risk because monochorionic twins share one placenta with vascular anastomoses.

**Complications.** *Maternal*: anaemia, pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm labour, antepartum and postpartum haemorrhage, caesarean birth. *Fetal and neonatal*: preterm birth, fetal growth restriction and **growth discordance** (a difference in estimated fetal weight of 20% or more is a trigger for referral), congenital anomalies, malpresentation and, in monochorionic twins, **twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)**, twin anaemia polycythaemia sequence, selective growth restriction and death of one twin with risk to the survivor. In TTTS, one twin (the donor) becomes hypovolaemic with oligohydramnios and a small bladder, and the other (recipient) is overloaded with polyhydramnios and may develop heart failure. Severe cases are treated with **fetoscopic laser ablation** of placental anastomoses. Monochorionic pregnancies need ultrasound every 2 weeks from about 16 weeks; DCDA twins have scans roughly every 4 weeks from 20 weeks. In uncomplicated twins, birth is recommended around 37 weeks for DCDA and about 36 weeks for MCDA (earlier, with caesarean section, for MCMA); follow current NICE guidance.

blocks.caption: Growth discordance between twins, where W is the estimated fetal weight in grams; 20% or more is clinically significant.

blocks.title: Recognising twin-twin transfusion syndrome
blocks.prompt: At 19 weeks, monochorionic diamniotic twins are scanned. Twin A has a single deepest vertical pocket (DVP) of 1 cm and the bladder is not visible; Twin B has a DVP of 11 cm with a normal bladder. Estimated weights are 235 g and 290 g. Interpret the findings and plan care.

steps.text: Chorionicity matters first: monochorionic twins share a placenta, so TTTS is possible. Twin A has oligohydramnios and no visible bladder (donor), Twin B has polyhydramnios (recipient): the oligohydramnios-polyhydramnios sequence.
Stage: the donor's non-visible bladder places the case at Quintero stage II (stage I has only the fluid discordance; III adds abnormal Doppler; IV hydrops; V fetal death).

Management: urgent referral to a fetal medicine centre; fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses is the treatment for stage II or higher disease in the typical gestational window (about 16 to 26 weeks); close surveillance afterwards and counselling about risks to both twins.

blocks.answer: Quintero stage II TTTS in monochorionic twins; refer urgently for fetoscopic laser ablation and close follow-up.

items: Previous spontaneous preterm birth and short cervix are the strongest predictors of preterm birth.
Steroids are given when delivery is expected, ideally 24 hours or more before birth; magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection before about 30 weeks.
Tocolysis buys about 48 hours; it is not appropriate with abruption, infection or fetal compromise.
Chorionicity, determined at 11 to 14 weeks, defines twin surveillance and the risk of TTTS.
Plan place and timing of delivery for twins with the multidisciplinary team.

blocks.title: The value of 48 hours
blocks.text: The aim of tocolysis is not to prolong pregnancy to term. It buys enough time for corticosteroids to act (ideally 24 to 48 hours) and for in-utero transfer to a centre with neonatal intensive care, both of which improve survival.

points: Preterm birth is birth before 37 weeks; spontaneous preterm birth, PPROM and indicated delivery all contribute, and previous preterm birth and short cervix are major risk factors.
Prevention uses cervical surveillance, progesterone and cerclage in selected high-risk women; acute management uses steroids, magnesium sulfate, tocolysis and in-utero transfer.
Twin pregnancy raises maternal and fetal risks; chorionicity determines surveillance, and monochorionic twins can develop TTTS treated by laser ablation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for spontaneous preterm birth in a current pregnancy?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: previous spontaneous preterm birth substantially raises the recurrence risk.
distractorRationale.b: Mid-twenties to thirties is not a risk age; extremes of age are.
distractorRationale.c: Nulliparity is not a strong predictor.
distractorRationale.d: Moderate caffeine intake is not an established cause.

questions.explanation: The history of a previous spontaneous preterm birth identifies women with a persistent predisposition such as a short or weak cervix or genital tract inflammation. It is the single strongest predictor and triggers cervical surveillance.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 20 weeks has had a previous mid-trimester loss and a cervical length of 17 mm on transvaginal scan. Which intervention is most appropriate to consider to reduce her risk of preterm birth?

options.text: Vaginal progesterone or cervical cerclage, chosen after specialist assessment

questions.correctOptionText: Vaginal progesterone or cervical cerclage, chosen after specialist assessment

distractorRationale.a: Correct: short cervix with prior mid-trimester loss is an indication to consider progesterone or cerclage.
distractorRationale.b: Routine antibiotics are not effective in the absence of infection.
distractorRationale.c: Bed rest does not prevent preterm birth and increases thromboembolic risk.
distractorRationale.d: Induction would cause, not prevent, early delivery.

questions.explanation: A shortened cervix indicates a risk of cervical insufficiency and early opening. Vaginal progesterone and cerclage have evidence for lowering preterm birth in selected women, so referral to a specialist preterm birth clinic is appropriate (check current NICE and RCOG guidance).

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of giving antenatal corticosteroids to a woman who is likely to deliver at 30 weeks?

options.text: To accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome and death
To stop uterine contractions for several weeks

questions.correctOptionText: To accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome and death

distractorRationale.a: Correct: corticosteroids induce surfactant production and structural maturation of the fetal lung.

questions.explanation: Corticosteroids cross the placenta and induce surfactant synthesis and lung maturation, lowering rates of neonatal respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage, necrotising enterocolitis and death. Maximum benefit occurs when birth occurs 24 hours to 7 days after the first dose.

questions.stem: A woman at 29 weeks with intact membranes is having regular contractions and cervical dilatation of 3 cm. Which situation would be a contraindication to giving tocolysis?

options.text: Suspected chorioamnionitis with maternal fever and uterine tenderness
The need to complete a course of antenatal corticosteroids
The need for transfer to a unit with neonatal intensive care
A normal fetal heart rate and a previously uncomplicated pregnancy

questions.correctOptionText: Suspected chorioamnionitis with maternal fever and uterine tenderness

distractorRationale.a: Correct: infection (and abruption or fetal compromise) are contraindications; delivery may be the safest option.
distractorRationale.b: This is an indication for short-term tocolysis.
distractorRationale.c: This is an indication for short-term tocolysis.
distractorRationale.d: Reassuring status does not contraindicate tocolysis.

questions.explanation: Tocolysis only buys time and is useful when that time is used for steroids or transfer. Where continuing the pregnancy is itself harmful, as with chorioamnionitis, abruption or fetal compromise, delay is unhelpful or dangerous.

questions.stem: A woman is expected to deliver at 27 weeks. Which additional maternal treatment before birth reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in the baby?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: antenatal magnesium sulfate gives fetal neuroprotection.
distractorRationale.b: Nifedipine is a tocolytic and does not reduce cerebral palsy.
distractorRationale.c: Erythromycin treats or prevents infection in PPROM.
distractorRationale.d: Atosiban is a tocolytic without a neuroprotective role.

questions.explanation: Magnesium sulfate given to the mother before very early delivery reduces the rate of cerebral palsy in surviving infants. Maternal toxicity monitoring (reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output) is required during infusion.

questions.stem: At a 32-week scan of dichorionic twins, the estimated weight of twin 1 is 1,800 g and of twin 2 is 1,350 g. Calculate the growth discordance as a percentage of the larger twin's weight.
questions.explanation: Discordance = (1,800 - 1,350) / 1,800 x 100 = 450 / 1,800 x 100 = 25%. This exceeds the 20% level that is a trigger for referral and closer surveillance, because it suggests selective fetal growth restriction of the smaller twin.

questions.stem: An ultrasound scan at 12 weeks shows a twin pregnancy with a thin T-shaped junction between the membranes and the placenta. What does this indicate and what follows?

options.text: Monochorionic diamniotic twins; ultrasound surveillance every 2 weeks from about 16 weeks
Dichorionic diamniotic twins; scans every 2 weeks from 12 weeks
Monochorionic monoamniotic twins; routine four-weekly scans

questions.correctOptionText: Monochorionic diamniotic twins; ultrasound surveillance every 2 weeks from about 16 weeks

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a T sign indicates monochorionic diamniotic twins, which need fortnightly scans to detect TTTS.
distractorRationale.b: Dichorionic twins show a lambda (twin peak) sign.
distractorRationale.c: Monoamniotic twins have no dividing membrane.
distractorRationale.d: Conjoined twins would not have a separating membrane junction pattern.

questions.explanation: A thin dividing membrane meeting the placenta at a T shape means the placenta is single and the membrane is only two amnion layers. Because monochorionic twins share placental vessels, regular scanning detects TTTS and growth discordance early.

questions.stem: True or false: twin-twin transfusion syndrome can occur in dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancies.
questions.explanation: TTTS results from imbalanced blood flow through vascular anastomoses in a shared placenta, so it occurs only in monochorionic twins. Dichorionic twins have separate placentas and are not at risk of TTTS.

questions.stem: A woman with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy asks how it differs from a singleton pregnancy. Discuss the maternal and fetal complications of twin pregnancy and how care is organised, and describe the additional risks if the twins were monochorionic.
markingGuide: Maternal: anaemia, pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, antepartum and postpartum haemorrhage, caesarean section, hyperemesis
Fetal and neonatal: preterm birth, growth restriction and discordance, congenital anomalies, malpresentation, perinatal mortality
Care: chorionicity determined at 11 to 14 weeks, regular growth scans, multidisciplinary team, planned timing of birth around 37 weeks for DCDA
Monochorionic additional risks: TTTS, twin anaemia polycythaemia sequence, selective growth restriction, death of a co-twin harming the survivor
Monochorionic care: fortnightly scans from about 16 weeks, referral to fetal medicine, laser ablation for TTTS
Earlier planned birth for monochorionic twins and discussion of mode of delivery
questions.explanation: Twin pregnancy places more physiological demand on the mother and carries higher rates of preterm birth and growth disorders. Monochorionic twins add placental vascular sharing, so they need closer surveillance and access to specialist fetal therapy.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old at 27+3 weeks presents with regular painful contractions every 5 minutes for 2 hours. Membranes are intact, the cervix is 3 cm dilated, and the fetal heart rate is normal. Outline her management and the rationale for each intervention.
markingGuide: Assess for infection, abruption and fetal wellbeing; take swabs and urine, group B streptococcus status
Antenatal corticosteroids to reduce neonatal respiratory distress, IVH and mortality, ideally at least 24 hours before birth
Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection because gestation is under 30 weeks
Tocolysis (for example nifedipine) with intact membranes for up to 48 hours to allow steroid effect and transfer
In-utero transfer to a unit with neonatal intensive care
Intrapartum antibiotics for group B streptococcus prophylaxis
Counsel parents and involve neonatal team; mention that regimens follow current guidelines
questions.explanation: At 27 weeks the greatest gains come from maturing the fetal lungs and brain and delivering in a unit equipped for extreme prematurity. Tocolysis is justified only to create the window for steroids and transfer, not to prolong pregnancy indefinitely.
